title: The rally still has a cash-flow test.
deck: My assessment after Wednesday’s close: renewed enthusiasm for AI helped stocks advance, but accounting profit and cash available to investors remain different tests. Meta’s newly released results illustrate the cost of building capacity, while a separate legal judgment adds uncertainty that should not be hidden inside an adjusted earnings number.

sections.title: The rebound is real; its durability is still a question.
sections.body: The Dow finished Wednesday at 52,856.09 and the Nasdaq Composite at 26,702.86, both higher. AP reports SpaceX gained 7.8% and Nvidia 2.5%, while Netflix lost 5.3%. My interpretation: investors are differentiating among earnings stories rather than rewarding every growth company indiscriminately. The counterargument is that a short rebound can reflect changing positioning as much as improving business prospects. I would look for cash generation and durable demand to corroborate the share-price strength. Meta’s quarterly results arrived after the cash close, so they cannot explain the earlier index gains; their implications belong to the next stage of the earnings assessment.

sections.title: Positive profit can coexist with negative free cash flow.
sections.body: Meta’s issuer release reports $32.79 billion of operating cash flow against $34.91 billion of capital expenditure including finance-lease principal payments, leaving negative $2.12 billion of company-defined free cash flow. Revenue grew 26% year-on-year. My assessment: strong sales do not by themselves establish adequate returns on the new capital being deployed. The positive case is that capacity investment produces future revenue and efficiency gains; the risk is that spending remains high while monetization disappoints. One quarter cannot settle that debate. The Toolkit’s DCF requires positive normalized unlevered cash flow: this reported, non-GAAP figure is not directly interchangeable with that input, and turning it positive merely to fit the calculator would conceal the investment risk.

sections.title: An earnings adjustment does not remove a potential cash cost.
sections.body: Meta’s earnings release includes a $9.89 billion charge for its earlier agreement with state attorneys general. Separately, AP reports a New Mexico judge ordered a $25 billion payment over privacy claims; Meta says it expects to prevail on appeal. My interpretation: these are distinct matters, not interchangeable descriptions of one charge. Neither a reported charge nor a contested judgment tells us that the same amount was paid in the quarter. The countercase is that the ultimate liability and timing can change. In valuation work, model conditional payment scenarios and avoid deducting an obligation twice if it is already captured in cash-flow assumptions or the equity bridge.

sections.title: Use the official curve consistently.
sections.body: The official two-year par yield rose to 4.81% on 21 October from 4.79% on Tuesday; the ten-year increased from 5.12% to 5.13%. My inference: Wednesday’s equity advance does not require a story of falling end-of-day Treasury yields. That does not establish earnings as the sole cause, and small daily moves are weak evidence of a lasting monetary shift. AP’s market wrap quotes a ten-year market yield of 5.12%; this dashboard deliberately uses the Treasury’s separately defined daily par series. For a DCF or LBO scenario, keep borrowing costs and operating performance separate: an equity rally does not automatically justify cheaper debt or a lower cost of capital.

watch: Track whether operating cash generation catches up with infrastructure spending; distinguish revenue growth from returns on incremental investment.
Keep the earlier legal agreement, the new judgment and any subsequent appeal developments separate. Do not assume a fixed payment date or count an obligation twice.
Judge subsequent earnings reactions against fresh completed sessions, rather than assigning after-hours announcements as causes of earlier index moves.
caveat: Codex’s original analysis, not Owen’s personal view or investment advice. The research cutoff above is actual ET/HKT time, not the scheduled run time. Wednesday 21 October is the latest completed US cash-equity session. Share-price changes refer to that session; Meta’s earnings release is subsequent information. Treasury observations are official daily par estimates, not executable yields or corporate borrowing rates, and can differ from news-service market quotes. Meta figures are from its issuer-authored PRNewswire release reproduced by MarketScreener because the direct investor-relations page was unavailable. Reported EPS is not an adjusted measure; the free-cash-flow measure is issuer-defined and non-GAAP. Legal developments are attributed to AP, with no independent legal conclusion or assumed payment timing. Scenarios are conditional, not forecasts.
